repository.title: Repository
repository.definition: A project’s versioned files and Git history. A local repository includes Git’s management data in .git/.
repository.example: The diagnostics repository records its source, tests, and deliberate checkpoints.

clone.title: Clone
clone.definition: A local copy of a repository with its own working files and Git data. Another clone does not share your uncommitted edits.
clone.example: Your laptop and a teammate’s laptop can hold different local states.

working-tree.title: Working tree
working-tree.definition: The checked-out files you edit and inspect. Editing them is separate from staging or recording a commit.
working-tree.example: The 250 ms editor version can differ from the earlier staged 500 ms version.

diff.title: Diff
diff.definition: A comparison between two versions of content. Always ask which two states the comparison uses.
diff.example: git diff compares working changes with the index; git diff --staged compares the index with HEAD.

staging.title: Staging and the index
staging.definition: Preparing content for the next commit. Git’s index holds the selected snapshot, rather than continuously following your editor.
staging.example: A second edit needs another deliberate add to replace the staged version.

commit.title: Commit
commit.definition: A recorded project snapshot linked to history. An ordinary commit records staged content in the local repository.
commit.example: A checked timing change becomes a checkpoint another engineer can inspect.

head.title: HEAD
head.definition: The name for your current checkout position, usually attached to the branch you are working on.
head.example: Here HEAD identifies the baseline used when unstaging a path.

branch.title: Branch
branch.definition: A movable name for a line of commits. Creating one does not create a separate clone or copy every working file.
branch.example: feature/status can advance while main still points to the original commit.

remote.title: Remote
remote.definition: A named connection to another repository. Push and fetch transfer Git objects and update references; they do not share an editor session.
remote.example: origin is the conventional name for the repository you cloned from.

fetch.title: Fetch
fetch.definition: Bring remote objects and reference updates into your clone without integrating them into your current working branch.
fetch.example: After fetching, origin/main can advance while feature/status and its working files stay unchanged.

remote-tracking.title: Remote-tracking reference
remote-tracking.definition: Your clone’s local record of a branch on a remote, updated by operations such as fetch.
remote-tracking.example: origin/main is not a live view that automatically changes your working files.

merge.title: Merge
merge.definition: Combine histories. A fast-forward can move a branch name; diverged histories may need a merge commit and conflict resolution.
merge.example: The status feature and sampler fix have separate parents in the integrated result.

merge-conflict.title: Merge conflict
merge-conflict.definition: Git cannot automatically reconcile part of the content. The engineer must resolve the intended behavior and then check it.
merge-conflict.example: Two intervals cannot both occupy one constant when they describe different tasks.

acceptance-criteria.title: Acceptance criteria
acceptance-criteria.definition: Observable conditions that define whether a change satisfies the request. They guide implementation, tests, and review.
acceptance-criteria.example: Sample count must accept 1 and 10, and reject 0 and 11.

test.title: Test evidence
test.definition: A check of specified behavior. Passing it supports only what it actually exercises.
test.example: A test of 5 alone cannot establish that the upper boundary 10 is accepted.

handoff.title: Engineering handoff
handoff.definition: The context, versioned result, checks, and remaining limits another engineer needs to continue the work.
handoff.example: Share the commit, intended behavior, test evidence, and any unresolved board assumptions.

pull-request.title: Pull request
pull-request.definition: A GitHub collaboration record proposing changes from one branch into another, with differences, discussion, review, and checks.
pull-request.example: Opening a PR does not by itself merge your branch.

git-vs-github.title: Git and GitHub
git-vs-github.definition: Git manages version history. GitHub hosts repositories and adds collaboration, automation, and project tools around that history.
git-vs-github.example: You can commit locally without GitHub; a GitHub PR coordinates a proposed integration.

issue.title: Issue
issue.definition: A GitHub record for a bug, task, question, or requested change. A useful issue explains the problem and expected result.
issue.example: The sample-count issue specifies the inclusive range before AI writes a patch.

ai-context.title: AI task context
ai-context.definition: The relevant goal, constraints, source locations, conventions, and checks supplied to an AI assistant. Generated changes still need review.
ai-context.example: Provide the range, relevant validator, existing tests, and a request to avoid unrelated edits.

continuous-integration.title: Continuous integration
continuous-integration.definition: Automated checks run when a project changes. The result belongs to the revision that was actually tested.
continuous-integration.example: A green check on an older commit does not verify your new patch.

workflow.title: GitHub Actions workflow
workflow.definition: A repository-defined automation process triggered by events. Jobs contain steps such as installing dependencies and running tests.
workflow.example: A pull-request workflow can check the proposed branch in a fresh runner.

review.title: Code review
review.definition: Evaluating a proposed change against its intent, correctness, maintainability, and evidence. AI review suggestions are inputs, not authority.
review.example: Compare the validator with the inclusive range and inspect the boundary tests.

release.title: Release
release.definition: A named delivery with a description and, where useful, versioned assets. GitHub releases are associated with tags.
release.example: A release note explains behavior, checks, compatibility, and known limits.

tag.title: Tag
tag.definition: A Git reference typically used to identify a specific version for a release. It is different from an advancing development branch.
tag.example: The delivery record should point to the intended tested commit, not merely latest.

revert.title: Revert
revert.definition: Create a new commit that reverses an earlier change, preserving the earlier record in history.
revert.example: A shared commit can be reversed without erasing its place in the team history.

ps.title: Processing system
ps.definition: The Zynq subsystem containing CPU cores and fixed peripherals. Its CPU executes your application program.
ps.example: A UART application can use PS peripherals without adding a PL circuit.

pl.title: Programmable logic
pl.definition: Configurable hardware circuitry in the Zynq device. Its configuration is distinct from CPU application code.
pl.example: An AXI GPIO peripheral in PL needs a corresponding hardware design and configuration.

driver.title: Driver
driver.definition: Software that uses a hardware interface. Driver code does not create the hardware circuitry it accesses.
driver.example: A GPIO driver must correspond to an interface present in the selected design.

xsa.title: XSA · Xilinx Shell Archive
xsa.definition: Vivado’s exported hardware information used to create or update software support. Bitstream inclusion depends on export choices.
xsa.example: A v2 interface needs the v2 handoff rather than a renamed old file.

platform.title: Classic platform
platform.definition: A Vitis Classic project combining hardware information with software domains and related configuration.
platform.example: Updating an XSA requires checking the platform that consumes it.

domain.title: Software domain
domain.definition: A processor-targeted software environment in the platform, such as a standalone domain with its support configuration.
domain.example: This curriculum uses standalone concepts, not a Linux or Unified IDE flow.

bsp.title: Board support package
bsp.definition: Hardware- and environment-specific support information, libraries, and drivers used by the software. It is not a complete application.
bsp.example: A BSP built from the old hardware description can preserve old address assumptions.

elf.title: ELF · Executable and Linkable Format
elf.definition: A compiled and linked program file on the host, consumed by loading or boot tooling. It is distinct from the contents already in CPU memory.
elf.example: Rebuilding app.elf does not automatically replace the program running on the board.

bitstream.title: Bitstream
bitstream.definition: A hardware configuration artifact used to program PL. It is different from the CPU application ELF.
bitstream.example: A software-only string change leaves the example’s hardware bitstream unchanged.

linker-script.title: Linker script
linker-script.definition: Configuration that maps program sections to regions in the target memory map. It does not choose host project folders.
linker-script.example: The linker can place application sections into the configured DDR region.

jtag.title: JTAG load and debug
jtag.definition: A debug/programming access path used here to illustrate loading artifacts into the target. A debug run does not establish power-on boot behavior.
jtag.example: A JTAG-loaded v2 program can disappear after power-on loads an older boot setup.

boot.title: Boot setup
boot.definition: The configured process and persistent contents used to initialize the system at startup. Exact components and media depend on the board and design.
boot.example: Updating host files or CPU memory does not automatically update boot storage.

artifact.title: Build artifact
artifact.definition: A produced file or result that another tool or engineer consumes. Its producer, inputs, version, and purpose matter.
artifact.example: The ELF and bitstream are different artifacts with different consumers.

reproducible-build.title: Reproducible project setup
reproducible-build.definition: Enough maintained sources, configuration, dependencies, and version information to recreate and check the result.
reproducible-build.example: An isolated .xpr or a file named final is not proof that a teammate can rebuild the design.

manifest.title: Delivery manifest
manifest.definition: A record connecting a delivery to its sources, tool and target assumptions, artifacts, and verification evidence.
manifest.example: Record hardware and application revisions separately and identify which board observations were actually made.

diagnostic-evidence.title: Diagnostic evidence
diagnostic-evidence.definition: Observed facts used to locate the first failing layer before choosing a repair. The observation’s scope and version matter.
diagnostic-evidence.example: Old output after a power cycle suggests checking boot contents rather than randomly rebuilding everything.

vcs.title: Version control
vcs.definition: A system for recording and comparing project versions so changes can be inspected, recovered, and combined. Git is a distributed version-control system.
vcs.example: Record a known diagnostics baseline before experimenting, then inspect the difference from it.

vivado.title: Vivado
vivado.definition: AMD’s hardware-design tools used here to describe, implement, and export the Zynq hardware design. They produce different artifacts from the CPU application build.
vivado.example: A hardware-interface change produces a new handoff and, when PL changes, an appropriate bitstream.

vitis.title: Vitis Classic
vitis.definition: The embedded software development environment used for this curriculum’s platform, standalone domain, and application concepts. Classic and Unified IDE flows must not be mixed.
vitis.example: Classic 2023.2 uses the Classic launch option; the curriculum does not claim a tested physical setup.

cpu.title: Central Processing Unit
cpu.definition: Processor hardware that executes program instructions.
cpu.example: The PS CPU executes the loaded application.

gpio.title: General Purpose Input/Output
gpio.example: A PL GPIO interface requires configured hardware.

uart.title: Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter
uart.example: The example application can communicate through a PS UART.

hal.title: Hardware Abstraction Layer
hal.definition: Software interfaces that abstract device-specific hardware access.
hal.example: STM32 HAL and Zynq support libraries have related purposes but different interfaces.

ide.title: Integrated Development Environment
ide.definition: An application combining code editing, builds, and debugging tools.
ide.example: The project tree is an IDE view, not the whole disk.

ai.title: Artificial Intelligence
ai.definition: Software assistance that can propose code and explanations; its output needs independent checks.
ai.example: Review the proposed sample-count validator against the inclusive range.

axi.title: Advanced eXtensible Interface
axi.definition: An on-chip interface protocol family used for connections such as PS–PL register access.
axi.example: A software write reaches an implemented PL register interface.

ddr.title: Double Data Rate
ddr.definition: A memory signaling technology; here the term identifies a target memory region.
ddr.example: The linker script selects the program’s target memory placement.
